Conclusions and clinical implications
Prior to 2005, depression and suicidality were not considered to be core or deﬁning clinical features of CTE (Fig. 2).
During the 20th century, depression occasionally was documented in the case histories of some boxers who had chronic brain
damage and presumed CTE (Critchley, 1949, 1957; Johnson, 1969; Mawdsley & Ferguson, 1963; Payne, 1968). When docu-
mented, it was reported to occur in association with an obvious neurological disorder, not as an isolated or primary disorder.
In the past few years, however, there has been a much greater emphasis on mental health problems, such as depression and
anxiety (Baugh et al., 2012; McKee et al., 2013; Montenigro et al., 2014; Omalu et al., 2011), being possible core clinical fea-
tures—with suicidality believed to be a “supportive feature” (Montenigro et al., 2014). Some former NFL players who have
died by suicide, and whose brains were donated for research, have been found to have the neuropathology characteristic of
CTE (McKee et al., 2013; Mez et al., 2017). Overall, however, as a group, former NFL players are at lesser risk for suicide
than men in the general population (Baron et al., 2012; Lehman et al., 2016). Researchers and clinicians are encouraged to be
cautious and circumspect when considering the clinical presentation of former athletes, and to not assume uncritically that
depression and suicidality are caused by speciﬁc CTE neuropathology. This represents a Procrustean and reductionist view.
Nonetheless, a subgroup of former football players experience depression (Gonzalez et al., 2010; Schwenk et al., 2007;
Weir et al., 2009) and they likely have episodic or frequent suicidal thoughts. It is reasonable to assume that retired football
players with chronic pain, depression, substance abuse problems, life stress, and ﬁnancial difﬁculty will be at increased risk
for suicidal thoughts and behaviors—regardless of whether they have small, medium, or large amounts of CTE pathology in
their brains. It has not been established that CTE neuropathology represents the substrate of an inexorably progressive
 338 G.L. Iverson / Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology 35 (2020); 332–341
neurodegenerative disease, or that depression is a core clinical phenotype of this neurodegenerative disease. Therefore, the
clinical diagnosis of CTE in people with depression, given its dire prognosis, might have iatrogenic effects and adversely
affect treatment. Those experiencing depression, distorted patterns of thinking, and substance abuse problems might be partic-
ularly vulnerable. Importantly, however, there are effective treatment options available for depression, suicidality, anxiety,
headaches, chronic pain, sleep problems, substance abuse, gambling, and life stress. These are all problems that occur in
some men in the general population, they likely occur in a minority of former football players, and they certainly are not un-
ique to people who have some neuropathology of CTE. Providing evidence-informed and evidence-supported treatments
might reduce suffering and improve functioning in former athletes with depression.
Conﬂict of interest
None declared.

symposiums. He has a clinical and consulting practice in forensic neuropsychology involving individuals who have sustained
mild TBIs (including athletes). He serves as a scientiﬁc advisor for BioDirection, Inc., Sway Operations, LLC, and Highmark,
Inc. He has received research funding from several test publishing companies, including ImPACT Applications, Inc., CNS
Vital Signs, and Psychological Assessment Resources (PAR, Inc.). He has received research funding as a principal investiga-
tor from the National Football League, and salary support as a collaborator from the Harvard Integrated Program to Protect
and Improve the Health of National Football League Players Association Members. He acknowledges unrestricted philan-
thropic support from ImPACT Applications, Inc., the Mooney-Reed Charitable Foundation, and the Spaulding Research
Institute.

Conclusions and clinical implications
Prior to 2005, depression and suicidality were not considered to be core or deﬁning clinical features of CTE (Fig. 2).
During the 20th century, depression occasionally was documented in the case histories of some boxers who had chronic brain
damage and presumed CTE (Critchley, 1949, 1957; Johnson, 1969; Mawdsley & Ferguson, 1963; Payne, 1968). When docu-
mented, it was reported to occur in association with an obvious neurological disorder, not as an isolated or primary disorder.
In the past few years, however, there has been a much greater emphasis on mental health problems, such as depression and
anxiety (Baugh et al., 2012; McKee et al., 2013; Montenigro et al., 2014; Omalu et al., 2011), being possible core clinical fea-
tures—with suicidality believed to be a “supportive feature” (Montenigro et al., 2014). Some former NFL players who have
died by suicide, and whose brains were donated for research, have been found to have the neuropathology characteristic of
CTE (McKee et al., 2013; Mez et al., 2017). Overall, however, as a group, former NFL players are at lesser risk for suicide
than men in the general population (Baron et al., 2012; Lehman et al., 2016). Researchers and clinicians are encouraged to be
cautious and circumspect when considering the clinical presentation of former athletes, and to not assume uncritically that
depression and suicidality are caused by speciﬁc CTE neuropathology. This represents a Procrustean and reductionist view.
Nonetheless, a subgroup of former football players experience depression (Gonzalez et al., 2010; Schwenk et al., 2007;
Weir et al., 2009) and they likely have episodic or frequent suicidal thoughts. It is reasonable to assume that retired football
players with chronic pain, depression, substance abuse problems, life stress, and ﬁnancial difﬁculty will be at increased risk
for suicidal thoughts and behaviors—regardless of whether they have small, medium, or large amounts of CTE pathology in
their brains. It has not been established that CTE neuropathology represents the substrate of an inexorably progressive
 338 G.L. Iverson / Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology 35 (2020); 332–341
neurodegenerative disease, or that depression is a core clinical phenotype of this neurodegenerative disease. Therefore, the
clinical diagnosis of CTE in people with depression, given its dire prognosis, might have iatrogenic effects and adversely
affect treatment. Those experiencing depression, distorted patterns of thinking, and substance abuse problems might be partic-
ularly vulnerable. Importantly, however, there are effective treatment options available for depression, suicidality, anxiety,
headaches, chronic pain, sleep problems, substance abuse, gambling, and life stress. These are all problems that occur in
some men in the general population, they likely occur in a minority of former football players, and they certainly are not un-
ique to people who have some neuropathology of CTE. Providing evidence-informed and evidence-supported treatments
might reduce suffering and improve functioning in former athletes with depression.

None declared.

for discussing or presenting research relating to mild TBI and sport-related concussion at meetings, scientiﬁc conferences, and
symposiums. He has a clinical and consulting practice in forensic neuropsychology involving individuals who have sustained
mild TBIs (including athletes). He serves as a scientiﬁc advisor for BioDirection, Inc., Sway Operations, LLC, and Highmark,
Inc. He has received research funding from several test publishing companies, including ImPACT Applications, Inc., CNS
Vital Signs, and Psychological Assessment Resources (PAR, Inc.). He has received research funding as a principal investiga-
tor from the National Football League, and salary support as a collaborator from the Harvard Integrated Program to Protect
and Improve the Health of National Football League Players Association Members. He acknowledges unrestricted philan-
thropic support from ImPACT Applications, Inc., the Mooney-Reed Charitable Foundation, and the Spaulding Research
Institute.

11	Background: Recent attention has focused on the optimal surgical treatment for recurrent shoulder instability in young athletes.
12	Collision athletes are at a higher risk for recurrent instability after surgery.

17	ferences (Pac-12 Conference, Southeastern Conference [SEC], Atlantic Coast Conference [ACC]). After gaining institutional
18	review board approval, 7 programs qualified and participated. Data on direction of instability, type of surgery, time to resume
19	participation, and quality and level of play before and after surgery were collected.

Return to Play After Shoulder Instability
Surgery in National Collegiate Athletic
Association Division I Intercollegiate
Football Athletes
R. Judd Robins,* MD, Jimmy H. Daruwalla, MD, Seth C. Gamradt, MD, Eric C. McCarty, MD,
Jason L. Dragoo, MD, Robert E. Hancock, MD, Jeffrey A. Guy, MD, George A. Cotsonis, MA,
John W. Xerogeanes, MD, ASP Collaborative Group, and Patrick E. Greis, MD
Investigation performed at the University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA;
and Emory University, Atlanta, Georgia, USA

Background: Recent attention has focused on the optimal surgical treatment for recurrent shoulder instability in young athletes.
Collision athletes are at a higher risk for recurrent instability after surgery.
Purpose: To evaluate variables affecting return-to-play (RTP) rates in Division I intercollegiate football athletes after shoulder
instability surgery.
Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: Invitations to participate were made to select sports medicine programs that care for athletes in Division I football con-
ferences (Pac-12 Conference, Southeastern Conference [SEC], Atlantic Coast Conference [ACC]). After gaining institutional
review board approval, 7 programs qualified and participated. Data on direction of instability, type of surgery, time to resume
participation, and quality and level of play before and after surgery were collected.
Results: There were 168 of 177 procedures that were arthroscopic surgery, with a mean 3.3-year follow-up. Overall, 85.4% of
players who underwent arthroscopic surgery without concomitant procedures returned to play. Moreover, 15.6% of athletes
who returned to play sustained subsequent shoulder injuries, and 10.3% sustained recurrent instability, resulting in reduction/
revision surgery. No differences were noted in RTP rates in athletes who underwent anterior labral repair (82.4%), posterior labral
repair (92.9%), combined anterior-posterior repair (84.8%; P = .2945), or open repair (88.9%; P = .9362). Also, 93.3% of starters,
95.4% of utilized players, and 75.7% of rarely used players returned to play. The percentage of games played before the injury
was 49.9% and rose to 71.5% after surgery (P \ .0001). Athletes who played in a higher percentage of games before the injury
were more likely to return to play; 91% of athletes who were starters before the injury returned as starters after surgery. Scholar-
ship status significantly correlated with RTP after surgery (P = .0003).
Conclusion: The majority of surgical interventions were isolated arthroscopic stabilization procedures, with no statistically signif-
icant difference in RTP rates when concomitant arthroscopic procedures or open stabilization procedures were performed. Ath-
letes who returned to play often played in a higher percentage of games after surgery than before the injury, and many played at
the same or a higher level after surgery.
Keywords: shoulder instability; return to sport; intercollegiate football

 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective case series of 177 shoulder instability surgeries in 153 NCAA Division I football players from seven Pac-12, ACC and SEC programs, covering the 2004-2013 seasons, with mean follow-up of 3.3 years. Of 168 arthroscopic procedures, 85.4% of athletes with isolated arthroscopic surgery returned to play, and return rates did not differ by repair type (anterior, posterior, combined or open). Players played a higher percentage of games after surgery (71.5%) than before injury (49.9%, P < .0001), and scholarship players returned more often (90.9% vs 65.5%, P = .0003).",

Only 9 open procedures were performed, so the open versus arthroscopic comparison is underpowered, and return to play does not measure recurrent instability directly.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 85% return-to-play rate as a reliable prognosis for their own athlete, when the study has no control group, covers seven programs, and does not measure recurrent instability.",

   "doi":"10.1177/0363546517705635",
   "abstract":"Retrospective case series of 153 NCAA Division I football players with 177 shoulder instability surgeries from seven programs. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery with no difference by repair type, and returning players played a larger share of games than before their injury.",
   "tldr":"In Division I football players, about 85% of those who had arthroscopic shoulder stabilization without other procedures returned to play, and returners often played in a larger share of games than before injury. Starters and scholarship players returned most often.",
   "methods":"Retrospective case series of athletes from seven Division I football programs in the Pac-12, ACC and SEC, covering the 2004-2013 seasons. Data included instability direction, type of surgery, time to resume play, and games played and depth-chart status before and after surgery. Return to play required clearance from medical and athletic training staff and a return to the roster. Chi-square and Fisher exact tests were used.",
   "findings":"Of 177 procedures in 153 athletes, 168 were arthroscopic and 9 were open bone-block operations. Return to play was 85.4% after isolated arthroscopic surgery, 82.4% after anterior, 92.9% after posterior and 84.8% after combined repair, with no significant differences. Starters returned at 93.3%, and rarely used players at 75.7%. Games played rose from 49.9% before injury to 71.5% after surgery (P < .0001). Among returners, 15.6% had later shoulder problems and 10.3% had recurrent instability needing reduction or revision surgery.",
   "limitations":"Retrospective design with possible recall and selection bias, no control group, and missing games-played data for two of seven schools (142 players). Open-surgery numbers were small (9), and return to play does not directly measure recurrent instability. The authors caution that depth-chart and games-played measures do not capture instability.",
   "practicalImplications":"For a collegiate football player with shoulder instability, surgery led to a high return rate in this series. Expect lower return odds for players who rarely played before injury (75.7%) and for non-scholarship players (65.5%), and discuss later shoulder problems, which affected 15.6% of returners.",
   "athleteDev":"Players who returned often played a larger share of games and kept or improved their depth-chart role after surgery, which can serve as a benchmark when planning roles. The study has no control group, so it cannot show that surgery itself caused these changes.",
   "rtp":"The series gives return-to-play rates after shoulder stabilization in collegiate football, with 85.4% returning after isolated arthroscopic surgery. It does not set safe timing, reinjury risk or readiness criteria, and it does not measure recurrent instability, so it is weak evidence for clearing an individual athlete."

}

It sets out impairments (range of motion, strength, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness) and a phased rehabilitation framework.",

 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the listed range-of-motion, strength and workload thresholds as validated pass or fail cut-offs for their own athletes, when the chapter presents them as guidance drawn mainly from throwers and other overhead sports.",

   "abstract":"Clinical review of return to play after shoulder stabilization in athletes who are struggling to return. It covers the wide variation in return rates, the lag in performance after return to sport, and the impairments and interventions that may explain poor outcomes.",
   "tldr":"Return to play after shoulder stabilization varies widely, and clearance by time alone misses impairments that matter. Rehabilitation should check range of motion, strength, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness before and during the return-to-sport progression.",
   "methods":"Clinical review chapter. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The chapter draws on published consensus statements, rehabilitation guidelines, return-to-sport studies and assessment methods, and sets out a phased framework with assessment techniques and exercise examples.",
   "findings":"The chapter reports return-to-sport rates of 63% to 100% after stabilization, with performance lagging return to sport by 6% to 25%, most in throwing athletes. Time was the sole clearance criterion in 75% of studies it cites. It reports that athletes who did not complete criterion-based return-to-sport testing were 4.85 times as likely to have recurrent instability after return, with a 22% recurrence rate versus 5% for those who passed.",
   "limitations":"Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method. Many thresholds it presents come from studies of throwers and swimmers, and the chapter itself notes there is no consensus on return-to-play criteria or on the use of ER/IR ratios in collision sports.",
   "practicalImplications":"Base the return-to-play decision on a test battery that covers range of motion (including total rotation arc asymmetry above 5 degrees in throwers), strength and endurance, neuromuscular control, kinetic chain mobility and psychological readiness, rather than time since surgery alone. Track workload with the acute:chronic ratio, while noting that the chapter's sources link ratios above 1.3 to injury in swimmers and overhead throwers.",
   "athleteDev":"Returning to sport does not mean returning to performance. The chapter reports that performance lags return to sport by 6% to 25%, so staff should track strength, rate of force development, endurance and workload through the advanced phase, not only clearance.",
   "rtp":"Clearance by time alone is not enough. The chapter recommends criterion-based return-to-sport testing and reports that athletes who did not pass it had more recurrent instability. It gives reference thresholds rather than validated pass or fail cut-offs, so it cannot clear an individual athlete by itself."

}

4	Return to Play and Decreased Performance
5	After Anterior Cruciate Ligament
6	Reconstruction in National Football
7	League Defensive Players
8	Connor R. Read,* BS, Kyle T. Aune,* MPH, E. Lyle Cain Jr,* MD, and Glenn S. Fleisig,*y PhD
9	Investigation performed at the American Sports Medicine Institute, Birmingham, Alabama, USA
10	
11	Background: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur commonly in football. Recent work has reported ACL reconstruction
12	(ACLR) as one of several orthopaedic procedures with unfavorable outcomes for professional athletes. The performance impact
13	to defensive players after surgery has not been quantified.
14	Purpose: To quantify the effect of ACLR on the performance of defensive players by comparing them to a cohort of matched
15	controls as well as to measure the effect of ACLR on athletes’ career length in the National Football League (NFL).
16	Study Design: Case-control and cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
17	Methods: Thirty-eight NFL defensive players with a history of ACLR from 2006 to 2012 were identified. For each injured player,
18	a matched control player was identified. Demographic and performance statistics were collected from the online NFL player data-
19	base. Players who returned after ACLR (n = 23) were compared with players who did not return (n = 15) using t tests and chi-
20	squared analyses. Similarly, players who returned after ACLR (n = 23) were compared with their matched controls with t tests
21	and chi-squared analyses. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was utilized to test for significant differences
22	between performance before and after the season of the injury for the players in the ACLR group who returned (n = 23) and
23	for their matched controls. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to test for differences in the rate of retirement between the
24	groups. For all analyses, P values \.05 were considered significant.
25	Results: Approximately 74% (28/38) of athletes who underwent ACLR returned to play at least 1 NFL game, and 61% (23/38)
26	successfully returned to play at least half a season (ie, 8 games). Athletes in the ACLR group who returned retired from the
27	NFL significantly sooner and more often after surgery than their matched controls. In the seasons leading up to their injury, ath-
28	letes who successfully returned to play started a greater percentage of their games (81%) and made more solo tackles per game
29	(3.44 6 1.47) compared with athletes in the ACLR group who did not return to play (54% and 1.82 6 1.17, respectively) and com-
30	pared with healthy control players (52% and 1.77 6 1.19, respectively). After the season of surgery, athletes in the ACLR group
31	who returned to play decreased to 57% games started and 2.38 6 1.24 solo tackles per game, while their matched controls suf-
32	fered no significant decreases.
33	Conclusion: Players who successfully returned were above-average NFL players before their injury but comparatively average
34	after their return.
35	Keywords: ACL; knee injury; sport injury; NFL

In-Depth


Return to Play and Decreased Performance
After Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Reconstruction in National Football
League Defensive Players
Connor R. Read,* BS, Kyle T. Aune,* MPH, E. Lyle Cain Jr,* MD, and Glenn S. Fleisig,*y PhD
Investigation performed at the American Sports Medicine Institute, Birmingham, Alabama, USA

Background: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur commonly in football. Recent work has reported ACL reconstruction
(ACLR) as one of several orthopaedic procedures with unfavorable outcomes for professional athletes. The performance impact
to defensive players after surgery has not been quantified.
Purpose: To quantify the effect of ACLR on the performance of defensive players by comparing them to a cohort of matched
controls as well as to measure the effect of ACLR on athletes’ career length in the National Football League (NFL).
Study Design: Case-control and cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: Thirty-eight NFL defensive players with a history of ACLR from 2006 to 2012 were identified. For each injured player,
a matched control player was identified. Demographic and performance statistics were collected from the online NFL player data-
base. Players who returned after ACLR (n = 23) were compared with players who did not return (n = 15) using t tests and chi-
squared analyses. Similarly, players who returned after ACLR (n = 23) were compared with their matched controls with t tests
and chi-squared analyses. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was utilized to test for significant differences
between performance before and after the season of the injury for the players in the ACLR group who returned (n = 23) and
for their matched controls. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to test for differences in the rate of retirement between the
groups. For all analyses, P values \.05 were considered significant.
Results: Approximately 74% (28/38) of athletes who underwent ACLR returned to play at least 1 NFL game, and 61% (23/38)
successfully returned to play at least half a season (ie, 8 games). Athletes in the ACLR group who returned retired from the
NFL significantly sooner and more often after surgery than their matched controls. In the seasons leading up to their injury, ath-
letes who successfully returned to play started a greater percentage of their games (81%) and made more solo tackles per game
(3.44 6 1.47) compared with athletes in the ACLR group who did not return to play (54% and 1.82 6 1.17, respectively) and com-
pared with healthy control players (52% and 1.77 6 1.19, respectively). After the season of surgery, athletes in the ACLR group
who returned to play decreased to 57% games started and 2.38 6 1.24 solo tackles per game, while their matched controls suf-
fered no significant decreases.
Conclusion: Players who successfully returned were above-average NFL players before their injury but comparatively average
after their return.
Keywords: ACL; knee injury; sport injury; NFL

"methods":"Retrospective matched case-control and cohort study. Defensive players with ACL reconstruction from 2006 to 2012 were identified from public injury reports and matched to controls on position and years of NFL experience. Performance statistics came from the NFL player database for seasons before and after the injury. Successful return was defined as playing at least 8 games after surgery. Analyses used t tests, chi-squared tests, repeated-measures ANOVA and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.",
   "findings":"Of 38 injured players, 74% (28/38) played at least one NFL game after surgery and 61% (23/38) played at least 8 games. Before injury, returners started more games (80.9% vs 52.3% for non-returners) and made more solo tackles per game (3.44 vs 1.77) than non-returners. After surgery, returners' games started fell from 80.9% to 57.0% and solo tackles from 3.44 to 2.38 per game, while matched controls did not decline significantly. Defensive backs who returned also lost starts and interceptions. Returners showed a trend toward earlier retirement that did not reach significance (P = .064).",
   "limitations":"Retrospective design using public media and the NFL database, so some injuries may be missed, and concomitant injuries, graft type, technique and rehabilitation were not recorded. Position subgroups were small, and no multivariable adjustment was made. The abstract describes retirement as significantly sooner and more frequent after surgery, but the results give P = .064. The abstract also reports non-returner values (54% starts, 1.82 solo tackles) that differ from Table 1 (52.3%, 1.77); the table values are reported here.",
